products.name: Anna's Hummingbird — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: An adult male Anna's Hummingbird on salvia. That magenta throat isn't pigment — it's feather structure bending light.
products.description:
An adult male Anna's Hummingbird on salvia. That magenta throat isn't pigment — it's structure. Microscopic layers in the feather bend light, so the color flares or disappears depending on where you're standing.

This one is painted at rest rather than in flight, which is how you almost never see them — perched on a salvia stem, gorget lit magenta, close enough to count the scaled green feathers across his back.
specs: Giclée print of an original watercolor
8×10 image, matted to 11×14 with a white bevel-cut mat
Signed and titled in pencil
Fits any standard 11×14 frame — frame not included
Printed locally in San Diego

products.name: Burrowing Owl — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: A Burrowing Owl mid head-tilt beside desert dandelion. One of the few owls you'll see in daylight, and it nests underground in burrows dug by ground squirrels.
products.description:
Burrowing Owls live underground. They nest in old ground squirrel burrows out in open grassland, stand about nine inches tall, and hunt at dawn and dusk on long bare legs.

This one is caught mid head-tilt — the gesture everyone who's met one remembers — beside a stand of desert dandelion.

In the 1860s, a naturalist wrote that burrowing owls stood on every little knoll around San Diego. They're gone from 19 California counties now, as the open ground they need gets developed. Where they hold on, it's usually because someone noticed. They nest on vacant lots and roadsides — if you spot one, report it to your local Audubon chapter.
specs: Giclée print of an original watercolor

products.name: Emergence — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: A monarch on showy milkweed — the one plant its caterpillars can eat, painted as a single system.
products.description:
Monarch caterpillars can eat exactly one thing: milkweed. Every monarch you've ever seen exists because a milkweed plant was standing there — a nursery, a food source, the place a caterpillar becomes something else entirely.

This painting puts them in the same frame, where they belong. A monarch resting against the broad leaves of showy milkweed under a deep blue wash. Titled Emergence for what the milkweed makes possible.

If you have the space, plant milkweed.

products.name: Frieda's African Violets — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: An oil painting named for my great-grandmother Frieda — a midwife, an entrepreneur, and a grower of African violets.
products.description:
Frieda was my great-grandmother. I grew up on stories of her — a midwife, an entrepreneur, and a grower of African violets. She went after the life she wanted and built it against the odds.

My mother always kept African violets. Now I do too. And when I came back to painting after a long time away, this is the flower I came back to. The one that started it all.

Painted in oil against a dark ground, the light catches what most people never notice about them. The leaves are furred, and you can see the fuzz standing out along every edge. The petals hold a dozen shades between white and deep purple.

The original was accepted into the San Diego County Fair fine art exhibit and stays with my family. This print is how it travels.
specs: Giclée print of an original oil painting
8×10 image, matted to 11×14 with a white bevel-cut mat
Signed and titled in pencil
Fits any standard 11×14 frame — frame not included
Printed locally in San Diego

products.name: Western Tanager — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: A Western Tanager on manzanita. That red head is a color he can't make himself — he eats his way to it.
products.description:
A Western Tanager on manzanita — an evergreen with urn-shaped flowers and small red fruits, which is how it got its name. Manzanita means "little apple."

That scarlet head is borrowed. Most red birds build their color from compounds they process themselves, but the Western Tanager can't make his. He gets it from the insects he eats, and those insects got it from conifer buds. The color travels up the chain — conifer to insect to bird — and displays as a beautiful red crown.

It's why you find tanagers in San Diego's higher mountains, where the conifers are.
specs: Giclée print of an original watercolor
8×10 image, matted to 11×14 with a white bevel-cut mat
Signed and titled in pencil
Fits any standard 11×14 frame — frame not included
Printed locally in San Diego

products.name: California Gnatcatcher — Matted 8×10 Print
products.short: A California Gnatcatcher on buckwheat — a federally threatened bird that never leaves the scrub it was born in.
products.description:
The California Gnatcatcher doesn't migrate. It lives its whole life in coastal sage scrub, and pairs hold the same small patch of ground year-round. Its call sounds startlingly like a kitten mewing — usually you hear one long before you see it.

This one is painted with California buckwheat, one of the plants that holds that scrub together.

Around 90% of Southern California's coastal sage scrub is already gone, which is why the bird was listed as threatened in 1993. Protecting the gnatcatcher has meant protecting whole stretches of Southern California hillside — save the habitat and you save everything living in it.
